https://t.co/JQpAkH0ydm

Two things here:

1. Market Awareness

It is not a must for success, but the longer I am in this business, the more I appreciate longer timeframe and fundamentals. The investment thesis is harder to invalidate on longer timeframe, and the invalidation condition on technical chart is also harder to trigger (& sometimes a bit too far from the current price - as one of the cons that comes with every single strategy).

Market Awareness to me is not describing what has happened in the market, but knowing and understanding what's currently happening in the world, and how it might impact on the market, and our investment. 

Ultimately you need price to collaborate on the technical charts, but this type of additional awareness/ information is an added advantage when properly dissected and utilised in good hands, as you would know where your focus should be, and if it is wiser to lean bullish or bearish in a grey zone amid the constant confusion and uncertainties, as some of the facts/data are hard facts. 

真的假不了，假的真不了。

2. Reasoning > Call Alert

It is never about following call alerts, or copying trade ideas. Every account can post some tickers, entry price and stop level. But think about it, these are actually all very personal. E.g. it doesn't mean I have to follow your picks if it is not within my cognition, it doesn't mean if I get a lower entry price than you it is a bargain/ higher means not doable, it doesn't mean I have to agree with your stops, or your position size ~~ because every trader/ investor is simply different.

I would be particularly interested in following your reasoning behind the trades though - to possibly uncover my blindspots in my own trades and to refine MY process, and if I agree with your overall investment thesis and risk reward perspective on the chart (which again can be different by timeframe, you might be looking at RR 1:3-10 while I am looking at a positive expectancy in 3 months - 12 months).

How I Separate a Healthy Pullback From Actual Deterioration

A red day does not automatically mean something is wrong.

Some of my best entries come from stocks pulling back while the bigger structure is still perfectly healthy. https://t.co/Wjt02iwBKm

The first thing I care about is the trend itself. If price is still respecting a rising 21dma structure, making higher lows, and the broader trend remains intact, I usually see weakness as something to investigate rather than something to fear.

The question is not “is the stock down?”

It is “what is actually breaking?”

I also look at how the stock behaves relative to the market and its group.

If the market is weak but the stock holds up better, that can be constructive. If the entire group is still behaving well, even better.

What worries me more is when the stock starts underperforming everything around it.

A healthy pullback usually happens inside a stock that was already acting well. It had relative strength, a strong group behind it, and constructive price action before the pullback started.

That context matters.

A weak stock pulling back is not the same thing as a leader giving back a few percent after an expansion.

This is why I do not use one moving average as a mechanical buy or sell signal.

The 21dma is important in my process, but I care about the whole picture around it.

A touch of the 21dma inside a strong leader is interesting.

A touch of the 21dma after relative strength collapsed, the group rolled over, and distribution increased is a completely different setup.

Then I look at structure.

Healthy pullbacks tend to remain organized. You see support respected, volatility contract, failed breakdowns recover quickly, or price starts tightening near an important moving average.

Deterioration usually gets messier.

Support starts failing. Rebounds get sold. Lower highs appear. The stock stops responding where it should.

Volume matters too.

A pullback on controlled or lighter volume is very different from repeated heavy selling and failed attempts to recover.

One tells me the stock may simply be digesting gains.

The other can tell me supply is taking control.

I also pay attention to time.

A healthy pullback can often repair itself fairly quickly. The stock finds support, stops making downside progress, and starts rebuilding.

When deterioration is real, weakness tends to persist.

That persistence matters. https://t.co/UgKnAkxyLa

So when a leader pulls back, I’m not asking:

“Should I buy the dip?”

I’m asking:

“Is this still a strong stock taking a normal pause, or is the character of the move actually changing?”

And just because a leader pulls back doesn’t mean the move is dead or that a full correction has started. Strong trends need periods of digestion too. The same applies to positions you already own — not every red candle requires action.

Sometimes the hardest part is simply trusting the structure and giving a healthy trend room to breathe.

That distinction—normal digestion versus genuine deterioration—is where much of the edge lies.

This is also why I like buying into support rather than chasing strength.

If the pullback is healthy, I can often enter close to a logical risk level and let the stock prove me right.

If the structure actually fails, I know fairly quickly that my thesis was wrong.

That asymmetry is what I want.

The mistake traders make is treating every pullback as either an opportunity or a warning.

It can be either.

The job is to read the evidence around it.

Market, Trend, Relative strength, Group behavior, Volume, and Structure.

Together, those pieces tell you much more than the red candle itself.

I'm going to challenge you, but I believe most newbie traders look at $MRNA right now and see a "bull flag."

That’s not necessarily wrong, but over the last 3+ years I’ve learned that the pattern name is almost the least interesting part of the chart. What I care about is what that pattern is telling me about the people trapped inside it, where supply is sitting, and who is going to be forced to act if price starts moving in either direction.

That shift (from memorizing shapes to reading pressure) is a huge change in how I see markets now.

When I ask “who’s trapped?”... I’m trying to figure out where traders are positioned poorly. For example, imagine buyers chased a prior breakout near the highs and then got stuck as price pulled back. Those traders become potential supply because a lot of them are just waiting to get back to breakeven and sell.

On the flip side, if shorts started pressing into weakness and price begins reclaiming important levels, now they’re the trapped side. I care about that because trapped traders create urgency, and urgency creates movement.

“Where are the stops?”... is basically me trying to map out where forced orders might be sitting.

If $MRNA is building a tight base and everyone can clearly see the recent low, there are probably long stops underneath it. If price breaks above a very obvious pivot, there may be short stops sitting just overhead. I’m not pretending I know exactly where every order is, but obvious levels tend to attract obvious behavior.

Think of it like a crowded doorway...if everyone needs to leave at the same time, things can move quickly.

When I ask “where did supply show up?”... I’m looking back at the spots where buyers previously got rejected. $MRNA pushed into the 170ish area and sellers smacked it back down. That tells me there is supply there.

But the next question matters even more: "Has that supply been absorbed?" If price keeps testing that area and each pullback gets shallower, volume dries up on weakness, and sellers stop making progress, that’s telling me the market may be chewing through those shares.

It’s like a wall getting hit over & over. Eventually, if it stops pushing price back, I start paying very close attention.

And then there’s “who is forced to act if this level breaks?” If $MRNA clears a major pivot, you can suddenly get breakout buyers entering, shorts covering, sidelined traders chasing, and trapped longs deciding not to sell anymore because price is finally working. That combination can create the expansion I’m always looking for. I don’t need to predict it with certainty...I just want to know where the pressure could accelerate if buyers start to show up.

That’s really the point of the original post.

I still use flags, pivots, EMAs, inside days, all of that stuf, but I try to see THROUGH the pattern now.

A bull flag isn’t valuable because someone named the shape correctly. It’s valuable because it may represent sellers losing control, supply drying up, buyers absorbing shares, and pressure building for the next potential leg higher. Once I started reading charts more like an auction between people instead of a collection of shapes, the market made a lot more sense to me.

So when you look at $MRNA (or any chart), don’t just ask, “What pattern is this?”

Ask:

-who is uncomfortable/trapped here?
-where are they wrong?
-where are they forced to act?
-which side is actually making progress?

That’s the lens I’m trying to build everything around.

I hope this shines a light on how I think! Godspeed.

In 1997, Mark Minervini won the U.S. Investing Championship with a 155% return.

Stocks only.

One of the most important patterns behind his approach is something you can spot on almost any chart:
- Strong prior uptrend
- Each pullback gets smaller: 25% → 15% → 8% → 3%
- Volume dries up as price gets tighter
- Supply starts disappearing as fewer sellers are willing to sell
- Breakout through the pivot as demand returns

Each contraction tells you something: sellers are becoming less aggressive, while buyers are willing to step in at progressively higher levels.

He calls it the Volatility Contraction Pattern (VCP).

The idea is simple:
When a stock refuses to go down while volume dries up, pay attention.

It may be moving toward the point of least resistance.

Tighter before higher.
